utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Thomas Laugel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Susa. May I remind that you are still --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Olmsted, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we have 65 ter 6688 on the screen. This is tab 176.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Susa.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to begin by finishing up with the issue of the military courts that were established in the Banija area back in 1993. What we have in front of us is a 19 August 1993 report from the president of the RSK Supreme Court to the RSK Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2 of the English we can stay where we are in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Milos Vojnovic reports that all judgements of the military court of first instance attached to the 39th Corps of the Serbian army of the RSK received until now have been cancelled ex officio. Mr. Susa, the military courts that you and Mr. Hadzic deemed to be unlawful were in the end abolished and their decisions rendered null and void; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That was along the lines of my previous thinking, but I have to remind you at this time I was no longer minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3298, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we may have 65 ter 1597.2 on the screen. This is tab 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, I want to return to the 28 April 1993 RSK Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got anything yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It appears it's not released, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It should now be released. And if we could turn to page 19 of the original, page 27 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, during the session, which you attended, Milan Martic gave a short speech about the work of the police in 1992 in which he states that: "The police have filed 15.000 criminal reports in 1992 of which 5.000 were for general crimes, while the remaining 10.000 reports were against 61.000 Croats who fought against us." Now, the 10.000 reports against the 61.000 Croats refers to cases involving crimes against the state under chapter 15 of the SFRY criminal code; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I don't know the exact numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Martic then acknowledges the low number of final judgements which he attributes to the judiciary. And, in particular, he states: "Therein lies the cause. It is not my fault that after three days common murderers are released, and there are many such examples. It is not my fault that judges who should uphold rule of law talk the criminals' relatives into writing petitions so that they may be released. They compete as to who will release such people faster. This is neither mine nor the police's fault." Mr. Susa, what Mr. Martic is saying here is accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that's not accurate and it's good that it's not accurate. Mr. Martic at this moment is trying to shift the blame for the police's failures and the job they didn't do, and we see that from this number of 60.000 criminal reports. And not a single case was recorded where our judges released murders to go free if the case files had been processed properly. We'll go back, if you have time, to the Djuro Kresovic case and you will see what it was really like. We did our job rather well but we were not able to proceed based on criminal complaints that were incomplete, completely improvised, without any evidence, just so that the police could cover their backs by statistics showing that they are doing something. It would have been very important, and that requires a serious approach by the assembly, if Mr. Martic had come up with specific cases where this was done, which judges were involved, so we would have been able to start the procedure to dismiss them or call them to disciplinary or other responsibility. Because what Mr. Martic is talking about here are criminal acts, and they were not doing their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Martic then acknowledges: "We," meaning the police, "are not angels. There are no two ways around it, but we have cleaned up our act. We did not have the time to vet the people who entered the ranks of the special purpose units and all that. We simply admitted our own to be police and that's that." Here, Mr. Martic is acknowledging that he had -- admitted persons with criminal propensities into the RSK police ranks; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could see the second page. I suppose you're reading already from the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, if we can turn to the next page. Yes, there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But, in essence, he is admitting that there were police officers with criminal propensities and they were allowed into the police force; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Martic knows that. I don't. The only thing I know - and I said that before and I'm saying it now - is that they either didn't know how to do their job or they didn't want to do their job. Now, whether there were also criminals among them, I'm sorry, but I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When he refers to "admitting our own to be police," he means admitting Serbs into the police; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we're not going to draw any fatal conclusions for that, such as that the majority of our people are bent on crime. He had a chance, just like I did, to admit into the service professional people, ten instead of 300, as long as those ten were able to do the job as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page in the English. We can stay where we are in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, in fact, you then responded to Mr. Martic's speech. And if we see a little bit into your speech, you state that: "It is certainly hard to be at the head of a formation which numbers over 36.000 people." The formation you're referring to is RSK police; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If I remember now, I had about 120, 130 judges in all the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And somewhat consistent with what you just testified to, you then state: "At the police, they have tried to make up for quality with quantity." And there you're referring to the low level of professionalism as well as the high level of criminality within the police force; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would not like to speculate about any crime. At that time I didn't have any evidence of that. All the information was superficial and this gathering was too serious for me to come up with such a claim. But in principle, I defended the positions of the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You then assert: "The thing that bothers citizens the most is perhaps not whether somebody was sentenced to a year, more or less, they are bothered by the fact that they are not safe in the streets, that shots are fired under their windows, that they are beaten and robbed in full view." Further on you state: "Unfortunately, I know them and so do you, but this does not have to cast a dark shadow on any of the sectors. Many individuals tarnished the uniform they wore." Mr. Susa, the known perpetrators of crimes to which you were referring to, who tarnished their uniforms, were members of the police, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to say it was not all about crime. They behaved improperly in other ways. They came to work half drunk. They committed traffic violations. They were responsible for various wrong-doing which made them really improper as police officers. I was aware of cases where I really thought that the person should not wear the uniform, but in the judiciary, people do not wear uniforms. They work in civilian clothing. We know all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And these problems among the police force that you described during your speech here, as well as here today, you informed the Ministry of Interior about these problems, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In a way that I thought was constructive, that it would not be pure criticism or provocation. I did that regularly, continuously, and the judges in the field did the same. They sent their complaints to the secretaries of the interior in the area in which they worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And yet here, towards the very end of your stint as minister of justice, those problems continued and that is why you gave this speech; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These problems persisted, and they were somehow provoked and you couldn't deal with them so easily. I was able to understand Martic too. There was a huge number of people carrying weapons. It was difficult to control. Not everybody is responsible, not everybody acts responsibly when they have a weapon. There were situations where people got drunk and kept shooting all night. The problems arose from the fact that law and order could not be established in such a broad area within such a short time. We pointed that out constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, the problem arose, as you said in the speech, because the police did not properly vet persons they allowed into the ranks of the police force; correct, isn't that [sic]?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would move to add the last two pages that I showed to the witness to Exhibit P3081, which is a partial collection of pages from the 20 April 1993 assembly session. So we would just moving to add these two pages that we've now looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, so far, the Prosecution tendered the parts of this transcript as the -- with the initial number by adding the dot and the further -- the further number behind the dot. And I would just suggest to do it today in the same manner because many parts of these particular documents were -- had been tendered into evidence as a part of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no problem with that procedure. I was simply going to suggest that we just add these two pages to the exhibit so there's not so many sub-exhibits relating to the same document, but I defer to the Trial Chamber as what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, there are maybe 15 or 20 such -- such cases as to this particular exhibit. So one more or less is not a problem, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we could do, Your Honours, if I may just respond to that, is the Prosecution would be happy to compile them all into one exhibit and we could simply substitute P3081 with the amalgamated version, and therefore, Your Honours, when it comes to reviewing the evidence, you only have to look at one document as opposed to, you know, five or six or 15. I don't -- but again, I'm happy to do it -- if that's the way it has been done, I'm happy to proceed that way too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Actually it is complicated because we also tendered one portion of this particular document into exhibit, and it would be good for the Trial Chamber to have this document in its entirety maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's for sure, Mr. Zivanovic. What we will do for the moment, and we can eventually take other measures afterwards, but for the moment we will admit those two -- these two pages under a new exhibit number with a dot original number. The dot original number refers then to the -- well, I suppose the P -- what is the number, Mr. Olmsted? P?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, it's P3081.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. That will be after the dot.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So I believe this will be P3081.3?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be .1 because according to our records, there's only been 3081 so far been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I was suggesting something else, Mr. Olmsted. I was suggesting giving this document a new P number and then dot original number. The original number being after the dot.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President, I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's what we will do. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3299.3081, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, in your Dokmanovic testimony, you describe the territorial organisation of the SBWS as a pyramid form. At the base of the pyramid were the local communes. Above them were the municipal Executive Councils. And then the SBWS government was at the top of the executive authority. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at 65 ter 1939.22.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a 12 August 1991 decision by Goran Hadzic. And through this decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it is not correctly interpreted. It is clearly said in the first paragraph of this document that the document was adopted by the Serbian National Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, I was referring to the issuing person at the bottom, which is -- shows it's Goran Hadzic. And through this decision, the Serbian National Council establishes the foundations for local administration in the Serb-held parts of the SBWS based upon the Serbian National Council declaration on sovereign autonomy. If we turn to the next page in the English, we see under item 3 that the Executive Councils were to discharge all functions of local administration in local communes. Now it was based upon this that the Executive Council was established in Baranja when Beli Manastir was taken over by Serb forces approximately a week or so after this decision; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that most of this is not familiar to me. I was not a member of the Serbian National Council. As for these decisions they made, I'm not sure they were really applied in practice because already a month later we built up this system quite differently. If you ask me specifically about Baranja and Beli Manastir, I don't know what they were applying there. I appeared in Baranja only a month later with a considerably changed concept of bodies of local and state administration. I could not comment on this. But, in any case, we did not rely on this at all when we were creating our new concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, when you arrived in Beli Manastir after this decision was issued, there was an Executive Council in Beli Manastir. Wasn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, in Beli Manastir, there were bodies that had been formed and elected back during the Croatian elections. So those were the same people who had been elected at local elections in Croatia of which I knew nothing. And when I arrived in Beli Manastir, that was after the assembly session where we were elected ministers, when the government was formed, and then with the assistance of my associates, I ran a check. That's all I was able to do because there was nothing else. These local communes we are talking about, they relied on the municipal seats that still existed in Croatia. The only assembly that still existed and that never stopped working was in Beli Manastir. And there, we got them to undertake that in the following period, they would harmonise all their documents with the decisions taken by the assembly. So if we are talking about the work of the municipality of Beli Manastir -- and you have to remember that even before the war you had the municipality and the Executive Board of the municipality, the executive branch. It was not a new creation that did not exist in Croatia before that. All this was already functioning and very familiar, and the people from Beli Manastir operated within that system.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The president of the Beli Manastir Executive Council, Borivoje Zivanovic, was not the president of the Beli Manastir Executive Council prior to the conflict, was he?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know that. That was something that I did not have to pay attention to. But I don't know really what was happening in Baranja before the war or during the war. I don't know everything that went on, other than what happened through the work of the Tribunals, the courts that were in Baranja, and because of the buildings that were preserved because they were of most use.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, you answered the question with your first sentence which is: "I don't know." And I ask you to try to keep your answers as brief as possible. Now, under item 4, it requires the establishment of local authorities where they do not exist. The SBWS government worked to establish those authorities in the months that followed as towns throughout the SBWS were taken over by Serb forces, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not just the pace that was crucial. There were places that we had in the beginning and we held them continuously for the most part. Nothing major changed there or no new places were added. Authorities were being set up with difficulty because we lacked the proper cadres to do it with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us take a look at D6. This is tab 183. And these are minutes from a meeting in Lovas on 30 October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, by 30 October, Serb forces had essentially taken over the villages in Western Srem with the exception of, perhaps, Vinkovci; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 2 of the English. We can stay where we are in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see under number 13 that you attended this meeting along with a number of SBWS government representatives; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn back to the first page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This meeting was also attended by local commune representatives and TO staff members from various villages in Western Srem, including, we can see under number 3, Ljuban Devetak; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 3 of both of original and the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see in -- I draw your attention to the bottom of the page. Mladen Hadzic discusses looting and plundering and states that the TO Staffs and civilian protection have a special task in this. The specialist services will deal with the problem of crime quickly and effectively. The civilian authorities must become organised as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we might have to turn to the next page in the original for the last bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic is acknowledging that it is the responsibility of the local authorities to address crime, at least with regard to looting and plundering, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. In the sense that they need to act when theft and robbery takes place, it's known who should be processing that. But they would need to appear in a preventive phase and to keep an eye on what's happening in their area. But other than reporting any crimes such as robberies and thefts to the police, they were not expected to do anything in this domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: He also discusses the need for civilian authorities to organise. Mr. Susa, the primary purpose of this meeting in Lovas was to discuss how the government can assist with that organisation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what we always did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we turn to page 7 of both the original and the English, we see that you spoke at this meeting. And you state: "The government members are visiting all settlements. Wherever there are government members, they are doing something usual." You're referring to the SBWS government members; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 8 of both of English and the original, we see that Bogdan Vojnovic, who I believe you have already testified was the SBWS minister of finance, reports that socially owned property is being transferred to the jurisdiction of the government and that co-operatives were being formed. He further reported that the government will appoint people to these enterprises. Now, the appointment of heads of the socially owned enterprises were subsequently made by SBWS authorities, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, they had to do that. There was no other way. This was the most efficient way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to 65 ter 6507. This is tab 151.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly requested by the interpreters to slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us is a list of main enterprises and appointed temporary heads dated 28 January 1992. The list shows that the Vukovar municipality Executive Council issued 49 appointments, including, if we can look at page 2 in the English, under number 23, Ljuban Devetak as head of the Lovas agricultural co-operative. Now these appointments were made consistent with what Mr. Vojnovic announced at the Lovas meeting, as well as the government's decisions on territorial organisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would move to tender 65 ter 6507 into evidence, as well as the earlier document, 65 ter 1939.22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object as to the document 1939.22 because the witness was not able to give any information about this document, and he didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. That document dealt with the issue establishing local authorities, organising local authorities, and though the witness was not able to speak particularly to that document, he was able to discuss or to testify about the process of organising local authorities. And the minutes of the Lovas meeting that we just looked at as well as this document that's in front of us confirm that, and so the Prosecution submits that that document is relevant to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In my understanding, there is no foundation for tendering of this document. Otherwise, through the one witness who knows just something about one document about civilian authorities, the party could tender into evidence all documents regarding civilian authorities disregarding whether the witness know anything about them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if I may just say something more. This is cross-examination. And during direct examination, the issue of establishing civilian authorities in the villages and municipalities was put into issue. And the document 1939.22 addresses that issue. Now whether this witness asserts that he is not -- familiar with it or not is, to a certain degree, besides the point because it goes directly to that issue and it is relevant in evaluating what weight to provide to this witness's evidence on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is just -- sorry. Just to point out that the witness spoke, indeed, about the civilian authorities but not about this particular period. It is 12 August 1991. And -- and because of that, I think that there is no foundation for tendering this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. There's only one document that is admitted and marked. Could you repeat the number, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That one is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3300, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now if we may have D19 on the screen. This is tab 131.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, this is the 20 November 1991 order from the 1st Military District Command that Mr. Zivanovic showed you during direct examination. Now, putting aside the issue of the date of this order, it is clear from the language of this order that the 1st Military District Command required that military town commands, to the extent they existed, co-operate with the civilian authorities, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified concerning Srbobran Bibic, who is referred to in this order. And if I could show you 65 ter 716, this is tab 292, and what I'm about to show you is a 26 November 1991 Politika article entitled: "Vukovar will not be abandoned."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I believe it's, yes, to the upper right of the original. Now, towards the end of this article, if we can go towards the last paragraphs of it, the report -- first of all, this is a report from Vukovar on 25 November 1991. And it reports that the SBWS government has "delegated Srbobran Bibic, as the chairman of the Executive Council, the mandate to make the necessary preparations for establishment of a genuine civilian rule in Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So already by 25 November when this story is being reported, Bibic was performing the duties of chairman of the Vukovar Executive Council; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look at the decision. I don't know whether that happened on that day, just on the basis of an article in the newspaper. According to what I remember, I think that he was appointed as the president of the Vukovar Executive Council a little bit later. But without the decision, I really couldn't comment on it. Perhaps all of this is correct. I don't know. I didn't read the article so I cannot really say anything about it. But if you were to ask me specifically when Srbobran Bibic was appointed president of the Executive Council of Vukovar municipality, I wouldn't be able to tell you unless I saw the relevant decision on his appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa I'm not asking you the date of his appointment. What I'm asking you is that he was performing the duties of that position at least by 25 November. In other words, even if he was appointed at a later date formally, he was performing the duties earlier. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that he was carrying out the duties but I don't know whether that was earlier or later. I cannot really say that. But at any rate, for a certain period he was performing those duties, but I cannot really specify the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And back on 19 and 20 November, Goran Hadzic was advocating that he be given this position, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th and the 20th? Hmm, I don't know that. I don't know that he was advocating that on the 19th or the 20th of November for Rajko Bibic to be appointed. I don't think he could have come in favour of that because only a few days later did the law on the local organisation, the territorial organisation, come out. Perhaps it was in some informal talk, but this could not have happened in any official form.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would tender this article into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object. There is no foundation. Because witness doesn't know anything about position of Srbobran Bibic on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that it has established enough nexus given that this was the issue with regard to the previous document as far as when Mr. Bibic was performing the duties of president of the Executive Council. The witness has testified that Bibic held the position. He's testified that it's at least possible that he was performing those duties even before his appointment, so we believe that the nexus has been established for the purposes that the Prosecution is tendering this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us have 65 ter 6049 on the screen. This is tab 133. This is a 11 December 1991 instruction from the 1st Military District Command regarding the request for use of abandoned property by representatives of the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, under item 1, the 1st Military District Command instructs its subordinate units to resolve all issues of this kind in co-operation with and at the request of the SBWS government, representatives of elected local organs of power recognised by the SBWS government or commissioners appointed by the SBWS government. Mr. Susa, this instruction is calling for co-operation which is consistent with the earlier 1st Military District order we looked at. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. Namely, if we were just to stick to what is written, then that is so. But in practice that was not actually so. It would have been good had it been this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It is clear that the 1st Military District Command, its position on the issue of civilian authorities, was that the Town Commands should co-operate with them; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3301, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You described last week the Ilok Town Command as a drastic situation. It was the case, wasn't it, that in many other towns and villages in Western Srem, the relationship between the military, the JNA, and the civilian authorities was one of co-operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Ilok area was completely uncooperative and that's why I cannot really say that. The Ilok outpost of the TO Staff --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear which TO Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- did not show any co-operation in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Which TO Staff did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojvodina. The TO Staff of Vojvodina. Mr. Belic was not a professional soldier. He was a reserve officer whom the Vojvodina TO sent to that function. So this the information that I had at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But my question to you was that putting aside your views on the Ilok Town Command and Colonel Belic, in other villages in Western Srem, there was co-operation between the civilian authorities and the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that's what happened. At the local level, from one town to the next, perhaps you could monitor this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at 65 ter 6107. This is tab 142.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a 25 February 1992 report by the 3rd Mechanised Brigade command which reports under item 1: "The Town Commands of Tovarnik, and Ilaca are in contact with the civilian and military authorities in the settlements every day. We monitor, advise, and help them in their work." This is consistent, Mr. Susa, with the role assigned to Town Commands by the 1st Military District; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To form the civilian organs of authority as well. This is something that we must not forget.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: To help them; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often, not. And this is something that you can see clearly from their orders and, let's say, obligatory instructions for conduct where they are told to form the civilian organs of authority in places where there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, you agree that where there are none, where there is anarchy, that something, someone has to form some kind of civilian authorities. If not the SBWS government, then the JNA has to step in to help with that process; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not so simple. That would be the most general interpretation of what could be implemented. We were not able to set up civilian authorities in all areas because of the definitive and clear position of the military authorities that, until further notice, they were exercising all forms of authority in places where combat action was going on. And this something that they used to cover themselves any time something that could not be completed or implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned combat actions, but by February 1992, there were no combat actions in Western Srem as you've testified to. At that stage, the JNA -- and again I'm putting aside for the moment the Ilok Town Command which you and Mr. Hadzic assert you had difficulties with. But putting aside the Ilok Town Command, elsewhere the JNA was doing its best to help the civilian authorities establish themselves in those villages and towns; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part within their remit and sometimes beyond that, and mostly not informing us about the objective or the needs of the co-operation but by specifically forming their own organs of civilian authority. They had their own officers who were especially entrusted with these issues. When I'm talking about combat, I don't mean that it existed specifically, but the army would constantly represent the entire area as an area where combat was being conducted or was just about to begin, which was not true. I agree with you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3302, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we may have D30 on the screen. This is tab 135.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, this will be the 23 December 1991 letter from Goran Hadzic to the Ilok Town Command which you looked at during direct examination last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page in the English only. We can stay where we are for the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic informs Colonel Belic of your appointment as SBWS government representative to the JNA. To your knowledge, was this the first letter that Mr. Hadzic wrote to the Ilok town commander?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it was not their first contact. The first contact was effected through me, through my verbal address to the colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other correspondence that Mr. Hadzic wrote to the Ilok town commander in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that this happened before this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question is: Even after -- after this letter, did Mr. Hadzic ever write again to the Ilok town commander, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic did not have to do that. They established a commission which carried out all negotiations and correspondence with them. This was Mr. Bogunovic, Mr. Vojnovic, Mr. Visic, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you or Mr. Hadzic ever write to the 1st Military District Command with regard to the issues that are raised in this letter?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not write to the command of the 1st Military District regarding the situation in Ilok. I wrote another letter to them, and that was only once. I think it was only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You're referring to your 27 November letter regarding the Sremska Mitrovica prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you or Mr. Hadzic ever write to the 1st Proletariat Guards Mechanised division command regarding the issues raised in this letter?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now if we can look at page 3 of the English, page 2 of the original. I believe this is the penultimate paragraph in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic informs the Ilok town commander that the SBWS government had decided to grant Serb refugees from Western Slavonia accommodation in Western Srem, which was a reiteration of its earlier position. Mr. Susa, when did the government make its initial decision to grant Serb refugees with accommodation in Western Srem? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was before we established that commission which included Vojnovic, Visic, and myself. Until then it was not necessary because there were no refugees. Refugees appeared just before this letter, after their conflict in Western Slavonia and they -- their arrival in Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How was the government's decision conveyed to the Serb refugees in Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That government decision was not conveyed to Serb refugees until the first attempts were made for them to come. This is one of the ways to create the right conditions, and at this moment, we had not yet had any direct talks with the refugees. We didn't tell them where to go. We didn't know how this whole thing would end and what resources we had at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at P3222. This is tab 182.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what I'm about to show you, Mr. Susa, is a 7 November Novosti article. It is entitled: "Accommodation provided," and it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can go to the bottom of the original, it's the middle article, at the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the article states that the prime minister of the SBWS, Goran Hadzic, yesterday issued a call to all Serbs expelled by the Ustasha authorities and who have been rendered homeless by the destruction of war, that they may temporarily settle in the SBWS, and that was in a statement that was received by Tanjug. So it was the case, Mr. Susa, that in early November 1991, Mr. Hadzic made a more general call for Serbs expelled by Ustasha authorities to settle in the SBWS; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this. And I'm not disputing it. You asked me specifically about Ilok of which I was in charge. I know what we did there. Generally speaking, he could have invited them at this time. There were already houses sitting free and there were places for them to move into. There were many Serb houses available and Croatian houses. I'm not disputing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, as minister of justice, you were aware that this was the policy of the SBWS government, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not disputed that it was the government policy to receive refugees. That's perfectly all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This policy even preceded the decisions to allow the refugees in Backa Palanka to enter into Western Srem; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such general decision. I don't remember that the government discussed what Goran Hadzic said here. But if it had been discussed, I would have been in favour of such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, prior to the SBWS government deciding to allow the Backa Palanka -- the refugees in Backa Palanka to enter Western Srem, the government did not issue any written decisions or instructions on how these Serb refugees should be admitted into Western Srem or how their houses should be allocated; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was precisely the purpose of the establishment and the work of the commission in which I was involved. We did that. The government assigned us those powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And Mr. Hadzic relocated you and Mr. Bogunovic, two of his ministers, to Ilok, to oversee the settlement of Serbs in that area because settlement was a priority of the government, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He moved primarily me and Mr. Vojnovic who did not have offices since the notorious Erdut. And Mr. Bogunovic had nothing to do anyway because he was no longer minister of the interior. He was just attached to us, and very often he was quite useless. Mr. Vojnovic and I had offices of our ministries in Ilok and these offices we didn't have before. We dealt with settlement as an additional activity to the other activities of our ministries. It was not our primary job.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us have P370 on the screen. This is tab 134. And what you'll be looking at is 23 December 1991 instructions from the commands of the 1st Proletarian Guards Mechanised Division. And if we could look at page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can see that on the same date that Mr. Hadzic wrote his letter to the Ilok town commander, Major-General Delic, who was Colonel Belic's superior, issued instructions to defer all settlement and return issues to the municipal civilian -- civilian authorities, or to the extent those authorities did not exist, to the SBWS commissioner or to the SBWS government. Mr. Susa, this is precisely what Mr. Hadzic was asking for in his letter; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These elements did not impose any obligations on the commission where I worked. The army's positions were sometimes in collision with ours. There was no developed methodology as to who would move into which houses. We did not think about which of the Croats left to join some armed formations and we did not decide that their houses would be taken over. We dealt only with practical issues, how many houses were available, how many people needed accommodation and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But, Mr. Susa, you're not answering my question. My question was just to the fact that in this order, General Delic is informing his subordinates to defer all settlement issues and return issues to the civilian authorities, and that is precisely what Mr. Hadzic wanted; isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But then I should like to warn you about the paragraph that says: "Town Commands should ensure, regardless of who issues the decision, and especially if it is the commands that do it, that the houses allotted to refugees from other areas to move in, even on a temporary basis, are first and foremost of those people who will most certainly not come back because of the crimes they committed. This is to avoid that the owner of an abandoned house appears after it has been let out, and even if he appears, there is at least some argument for justification."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That seems to be a sensible order, doesn't it, Mr. Susa?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree that it's that sensible. It's a bit contradictory.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at P1932. This is tab 136. And this is the 25 December 1991 response of the Ilok town commander to Mr. Hadzic's 23 December letter. And if we can look at page 2 of the English. We can stay where we are on the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Colonel Belic writes: "I must admit that I expected there would be comprehensive, primarily planned and organised involvement by members of the government of the Serb District in connection with the settlement of refugees from Western Slavonia. We must quickly leave our illusions behind and be completely engaged in resolving the problems. That is why I assumed that the SAO government would form an immigration department, as part of a relevant ministry, which would be in contact with the military authorities, form offices for handling transport and accommodation in vacant houses, and appoint representatives who would deal with the refugees' social security, et cetera." He then encourages Mr. Hadzic to begin resolving these issues. Mr. Susa, it would have been better for the SBWS government to have organised the sort of things that Colonel Belic is raising in this letter before passing the decision allowing Serbs to enter into Western Srem, wouldn't it have been?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that you are not right for several reasons regarding this letter by Colonel Belic. This letter actually tells us about many things that Colonel Belic should have been doing and wasn't. First, what he says about houses being listed, that's not true. At this point in time, they had already moved people into more than a hundred buildings. He is writing this letter although at the same time there are proposals sitting on his desk as to what should be done, and he is writing this for our education; whereas in the previous letter you showed me, it is written clearly what he failed to do, what he should have done, and what we should have done. And now he is suggesting us to us what we should be doing. And all this time, he is keeping us out of Ilok and not letting us do any of the things that we proposed. You know why he is writing this letter? Because he knows that everyone knows what had been going on in Ilok, and he is not keeping any secrets anymore because there are no secrets to keep. He knows that all the thieving in Ilok is well-known to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: On page 3 of this document, both the English and the original, Colonel Belic writes: "In order to overcome problems and to resolve the most important issues quickly, effectively, and in a planned and sound manner, I place my command at your disposal." Did Mr. Hadzic share this letter with you back in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it and I read it, and I was very glad that Colonel Belic realised finally all his mistakes. And, of course, in the period that followed, he failed to implement any of these things. This is a political letter, equal to a pamphlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have P1709 on the screen. This is tab 137. P1709, tab 137.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a 29 December 1991 letter that you wrote, Mr. Susa, and you address the letter to "Colonel." That was Colonel Belic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know if he was still there. You will see when we get the record from that meeting in Borac. I'm not sure that Colonel Belic was there. I believe he had been replaced by that time. It was somebody else probably in the rank of colonel. But I didn't know the name, so I just wrote "colonel."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, at any rate, you invited the colonel to a meeting to be held that was being organised by the SBWS commission for the next day, so for the 30th of December, which would be attended by representatives of the Vukovar Executive Council and all settlements where temporary accommodation is being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to P1710, tab 138.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, it doesn't say they were being implemented. It says: "Your presence would contribute" -- now we have moved from that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May the witness have the opportunity to read the document and complete his answer. Previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The previous document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have P1709 on the screen again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to be quick. I'm saying: "Your presence would help clearly define problems and find ways to resolve it and also to the undisturbed completion of this difficult but humane mission." I'm just saying that it could be organised in this way. As far as we are concerned, I know for a fact that we had not started any settlement yet at this point. We were just preparing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, you are going well beyond my question which was simply that you invited the colonel to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So let's please move on to the next document, which is P1710.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this is a report by the JNA but it's with regard to the meeting that you organised. And we can see at the beginning of the document in the second paragraph that from the military, from the -- the army, two colonels showed up, both Colonel Milos Miljkovic and Colonel Milan Belic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now the SBWS government labelled the Serbs who were coming to the Western Srem area as refugees from Western Slavonia. But in many cases, the persons coming were not refugees; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not refugees. They had been expelled. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at P1818.1. This is tab 27. This is a 6 December 1991 DB Serbia report. And if we could turn to page 3 of the English, page 2 of the original, it reports that: "The Belgrade Radio and Television are having a negative effect on the soldiers and population as they were calling on people to settle temporarily in Eastern Slavonia, which resulted in the area being abandoned."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, this is referring to the broadcasts that were being made at the behest of the SBWS government, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. We did not wield such influence. You skipped the first page. There was an interesting sentence but I'm not going to come back to that. From that we see that Ustashas had attacked their villages. I'm not using the term "Ustasha" myself. I saw it in the report. As for your claim that we organised broadcasts to instigate these people to come, no, that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, again, Mr. Susa, you answered my question with your first sentence: "Of course not." The report then states that the announcements have caused Serb soldiers and police from Western Slavonia to leave the front and go to Eastern Slavonia, Beli Manastir, Ilok, and other towns where their housing an employment problems could resolved. Again, I ask: Some of the Serbs coming to Western Srem fell into that category, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that. I don't know how many people got their information through the media or if they had electricity at all. I remember programmes where we invited --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I cannot remember any programmes wherein we invited people to leave Western Slavonia and come live with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at 1D1400. This is tab 257.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What I'm about to show you, Mr. Susa, is a 29 September 1993 Official Note of an interview of Zoran Pendic. And if we can look at paragraph 3, this individual states that he arrived in Krajina on 20 September 1991 with 23 other volunteers from Smederevska Palanka and joined the Guards Brigade in fighting in Vukovar and other places in Western Srem. Smederevska Palanka is in Serbia, correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look at the paragraph 4, the next paragraph, it states: "At the end of the war, some time in March 1992, he took up residence in Nijemci where he was given a Croatian house to live in." Nijemci is near Tovarnik, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the left of Tovarnik when you travel towards Vinkovci, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So it was the case that Serbs from Serbia who served as volunteers in Western Srem were also given houses; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, but they shouldn't have. This person does not fall into the category of refugees or displaced persons. This was not under our jurisdiction. I don't know from whom he received that house. Probably from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3303, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted. Mr. Susa, we'll take the first break, 30 minutes. We'll be back at 11.00. Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Before we bring the witness in, a short oral ruling. The Trial Chamber heard the Defence submission about additional time for proofing of three witnesses. The Trial Chamber is not convinced that it is reasonable to ask more time, more than three days for proofing of each of these witnesses, and, therefore, the request is denied. And in light of this, the Chamber sees no reason to alter the schedule of the manner through which these witnesses should be heard as requested by the Defence and it expects no delay in the trial schedule. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, just for one clarification as to the cost of expenses of this witnesses if they come as planned. Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We don't interfere with that, Mr. Zivanovic. We don't -- we don't think you need more than three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But I don't know what's about the costs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There is no issue about the costs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was. Because they are scheduled to come and it -- is it mean that I have to reschedule my -- my plan for their arrival to The Hague? I'm not informed about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If your actual schedule is for more than three days --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- you should, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I should need, what? To pay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No. To -- to let them come for three days and not more or whatever other -- whatever other measures you want to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, but it is really unclear for me. If they come here and I have -- I'm really not -- not sufficiently informed about what I have to -- whether I have to pay their stay in The Hague if I meet them for more than three days. That's only issue is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It isn't a matter for us, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You organised your Defence as you wish, and you know what VWS intends to do with your -- with your witnesses and with the time they are here. And all the rest is not for us to decide upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. But I -- as far as I understood, I had to address you for -- for this interpretation, but, okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness may be brought in. Sorry, sorry -- oh. Yes. I'm sorry about that. The witness is already in. Mr. Susa is there, and Mr. Olmsted is ready to proceed. Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have on the screen 65 ter 5910.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, what's in front of you is a decision of the SBWS Executive Council dated 20 July 1992. Were you aware of this decision by the SBWS Executive Council establishing an SBWS committee for refugees?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really all that well informed about it, but I assumed that it's all correct. But this was not in the domain of my work, so I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, if you don't know about this decision, I won't ask any questions about it. While you were --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was already a member of the RSK government so I don't know anything about the work of the District Council in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: While you were in Western Srem, you were aware that civilian authorities in some of the Western Srem villages were pressuring the remaining non-Serb population to move out of the area; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that as a specific fact, but there was talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at 1D3485. This is tab 278. And this is a ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would that be a confidential document, Mr. Olmsted? Which -- what is the tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: 278. And it may be, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It may be, or it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm going to check right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The previous document Mr. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry. The Registrar tells me that the previous document has a Rule 70 indication on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. But I don't believe it would apply to this document which is a totally separate -- it is a part of that larger document which had protection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, so this --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- but this was an attachment to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So there's no problem with that one. And we do not broadcast this one, is that sufficient? Or should we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we -- it's a Defence document but perhaps we should go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have P372 on the screen. This is tab 140.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what you are about to look at is an 11 February 1992 memorandum from the Central Settlement Committee to the Mohovo local commune. First of all, could you look to -- as far as the issuing parties at the very bottom, who -- who is listed under number 2? Our translation doesn't indicate who it is.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Milorad Visic, a member of the Executive Council of the municipality of Vukovar. It's Dr. Milorad Visic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now we see at the very top it's written: "Ministry of Justice." Did you write this memorandum?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I did. We didn't have the proper memoranda so we used mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, you indicate that the Mohovo local commune submitted a proposal to the Central Settlement Committee to move out unwanted Croats because of their connections with members of the HDZ and ZNG. And in response to this proposal, the committee informs the local commune that they: "... have all the necessary authorities to make decisions about which citizens of the local commune are allowed to live in the territory and which are not." You next inform the commune that the Serbian District has not adopted any decisions regarding moving out Croats from the Serbian District because it is obvious that nationality alone doesn't present sufficient grounds. At this time, you were aware that Croats were being expelled from villages in the SBWS solely based on their ethnicity and that is why you included the statement that ethnicity alone isn't sufficient; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, your conclusion is the opposite of what is written here. I explained exactly how this letter was drafted, and this is the only document in which we touched upon the subject of future moving people out. We usually avoided that but this was a specific circumstance explained by the people from Mohovo. This was not classical moving -- classic moving out, if we wanted to really discuss this matter. People were leaving for different reasons. One of them was of an economic nature. And then we also explained that no one can be expelled or leave an area just because they were a Croat or a Serb. That is quite clear. There were also requests by Serbs to leave the area, and that is something that we also need to mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So it's your assertion that in the time of writing this memorandum you weren't aware that non-Serbs were being expelled solely based on their ethnicity. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In instances when Croats were expelled, I don't know what the reasons were for that. Perhaps it wasn't the main reason. Perhaps it was easier to get to their property if they were Croats. There was no particular criteria that could be applied on the work of the commission in respect of the desire to move out as many Croats as possible. It was explicitly said: Get off our back, you and the army, and we're going to do what we need to do. So I think that the actual resettlement of people from Mohovo never took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: As the SBWS government's attorney, you knew that a blatantly, openly illegal policy of expulsions, if exposed by UNPROFOR or the international media, would result in significant legal problems for the government; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the event that we did that, that's quite possible. However, we did not expel anyone, and there is no evidence of that. We were not expelling anyone in this correspondence either. We are informing the local communities that in all future actions they need to report to us. Had they done that, then we would have considered what we should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, you then state: "However, should the organs of your MZ establish that these individuals have violated the law and order of the Serbian District, if there is reliable information that they have collaborated with the enemy and the Ustasha authorities, and if it is established that their actions are still motivated by such positions and beliefs, then the competent organs of the MZ are not only entitled but required at the initiative of the inhabitants of the MZ and the organs of the MZ to resolve all issues related to the status of individuals residing in their territory; that is, they are entitled and required to withhold from such individuals their right to stay or permanently reside in the MZ." The government's position was, Mr. Susa, to leave it to the village authorities to decide whether reliable information existed that a non-Serb was an enemy or Ustasha collaborator and therefore should be removed from their local commune; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Is it -- is it citation from the document that it was government position or it was just the question of the counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought it was obvious. It is the question I am putting to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It was the government's position, wasn't it, Mr. Susa?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the position of the central commission regarding this particular individual case. There were no other positions in any other settlement. This was done ad hoc because of the enormous problems that were happening in Mohovo and there was a threat of escalation and a possibility of casualties. This is the way in which we calmed this down, and we put them in a position that they themselves needed to discuss this. They did not make any decisions on this matter, and ultimately they didn't decide anything. But the fact is that in Mohovo, the situation exceeded the bounds that could be controlled. We had the authority in this respect. We behaved in a responsible manner, and this is an example of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You were representatives of the SBWS government in Western Srem. When you wrote this memorandum, you were speaking on behalf of the government, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't dispute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what you state in this memorandum would apply equally to other local communes, for instance, such as Mirkovci, if they encountered the same situation where there were Croats or other non-Serbs that were perceived to be a danger to that community; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really speak about that now. This was not a memorandum for everyone. This was specifically addressed to the local commune in Mohovo. This was not a general position. And I note that, for me, the key paragraph was the last paragraph, as far as I'm concerned, that nothing could happen or be done because they were obliged to report to us or to inform us first about anything that they were intending to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, once moved out of the area, the houses of non-Serbs were allocated to Serbs arriving in the area; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For temporary use, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And although the provision of housing to the arriving Serbs was labelled by you and the SBWS government as temporary, the moving out of the non-Serb population from the SBWS was intended to be permanent, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not our intent. It was not our intent at all. And, in particular, it was not a permanent intent of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The non-Serbs, to the extent they were moved out because they were deemed to be enemy or Ustasha collaborators, as you mentioned in this memorandum, they were not allowed to return, were they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not stated anywhere. It's very difficult to say who is guilty and who is not until that is proven. Proceedings were held when people were supposed to be moving in, and it was very easy to prove if anybody took part in any formations or not. We had special instructions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And we saw during your direct examination the decision on the return of -- returns to the RSK. And that was to be done by the police, the very police that you have testified were acting unprofessionally in the 1992 and 1993 time-period; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was supposed to be done by police officers who were performing their job in a legal and professional manner. Whenever I encountered a case when the police were not professionally and properly carrying out their job, then we would take measures. I would not agree that all the policemen were carrying out their jobs in an unprofessional, incorrect manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What measures did you take?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would report that to their superiors in written reports, noting their specific behaviour if -- and if there were elements for the commission of a crime, then we would initiate proceedings. This is part of the job of the organs of internal affairs. The residence of a specific person in a specific area is still part of their remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Non-Serbs who were charged with chapter 15 or 16 crimes under the SFRY Criminal Code were also not allowed to return because, if they did, they would face detention, prosecution, and possibly eventual deportation; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would see how the interrogation proceedings would end, as to what they did and what they did not, in the same way the request on the part of Croats regarding Serbs on the Croat side would be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Last week when you testified - this is transcript page 12077 - you said that those charged with crimes were banned from returning to the RSK. Do you stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crimes and misdemeanours are not quite the same things. I would not forbid those who committed crimes from returning. The only thing that would happen would be that they could be tried for those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at L1. This is tab 31. And if we could turn to page 15 of the English, page 5 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is the Law on Enforcement of the Constitutional Law in the SBWS. And if we look at Article 5, it states that the inviolability of private property did not apply to persons whose property is seized based on special terms due to their subversive activities in the period of fighting on the territory of the Serbian District. Mr. Susa, non-Serbs who had their property seized because they were considered to have participated in subversive activities, they lost their property and had nothing to return to in the SBWS. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's completely incorrect. Those property was confiscated temporarily, and in the end, they all returned to their houses that had not been destroyed. At the time when this property is made available for someone else to use, the ownership rights are not changed. It is still the property of the Croat who had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you say they returned to their property, they returned to their property after the reintegration into Croatia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly they were in a much better position than Serbs who could not return because their property had not been preserved. Their property was preserved, and they had something to come back to. That's what we managed to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at P133. This is tab 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Non-Serbs who signed a voluntary departure document, such as this one that's in front of you, they also lost their rights to their private property once they left the SBWS; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody lost the right to their private property. Not those who left voluntarily, nor those who had allegedly been expelled. Nobody later had any problem to prove their ownership over property. We never called that into question, and we banned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you testified last week that the Croat authorities placed as a precondition for the return of Croats to the SBWS that the Croatian authorities be re-established in the area; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 5224. This is tab 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is an announcement published in the Belgrade Tanjug on 17 August 1992, and we see that Mr. Milanovic, the assistant RSK defence minister, calls the announcement that a group of refugees from Croatia will arrive in the SBWS the next day "yet another deception of the Croatian government." And he then goes on to state that both sides must give consent before refugees return. Mr. Susa, in 1992, 1993, the Croatian government was pushing for the return of Croats to the RSK; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
