utterances.text: They tried, but they had not undertaken to do that under the Vance Plan. The Vance Plan gave equal rights to both Serbs and Croats. We were trying to get Serbs to come back, and the Croats tried to get Croats to come back. There was something wrong with that. Both sides should have agreed for everyone to return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3305, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we may have D224 on the screen. This is tab 144.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic showed you this document last week. Now, under this mandatory instruction to the commission for temporary moving in as well as other state organs dated 28 September 1992, by its language, only contracts for exchange of property certified by courts outside the RSK were rendered null and void. In other words, contracts certified by the RSK courts were valid. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid you haven't understood this mandatory instruction. I am prohibiting the courts in RSK to conclude any contracts on purchase or exchange of property. It's clearly written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps we have a translation error then. Because underneath the capitalised "Obligatory work instruction to the commission for temporary moving in and other state organs," it is written: "All verbal agreements and contracts certified by courts with headquarters outside the Republic of Serbian Krajina ..." and continues from there. Is that what it states?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what is written there. But it's not the point. It's not the essence. It's only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then if we look three paragraphs below that, you write: "On the other hand, exchange and purchase/sale are allowed to all citizens of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and all contracts must be certified by authorised courts with headquarters in the Republic." In other words, the RSK courts; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So I put to you that this instruction ensured that the RSK authorities controlled how property was distributed in the SBWS, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was to stop exchanges and swaps that had already begun under suspicious circumstances and were certified on different sides. This was our attempt to go against these bargains wherein somebody would be given something for temporary use. We just did not want to participate in the change of ownership rights. We did not want to approve purchases and sales under suspicious circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The justification you provide in this mandatory instruction was to protect citizens whose property was seized or destroyed in the Republic of Croatia. In other words, this instruction was aimed and protecting Serbs who had come to settle in the SBWS; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To some extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's the only justification you provide in the document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not the only justification. We definitely knew that at that time there were already ongoing sales of Serb property in Croatia and that was disputable. Whereas the property of Croats in the Krajina was regulated by rules --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, you went way too fast for the interpreters. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The last bit of your answer we need for the record.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The property that Croats abandoned leaving for Croatia was not subject to purchase or sale because it had the status of property temporarily given to someone else to use. Nobody was able to buy it. And by virtue of that fact, the property of ethnic Croats was sufficiently protected. There wasn't -- there was not a single case recorded of any property being sold as long as it was recorded as property temporarily given to someone to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us have 65 ter 1597.2 on the screen. Tab 82. And if we could -- again, this is the transcript from the 20 April 1993 RSK Assembly session. And if we turn to page 12 of the English, page 8 of the original. We see a speech from Deputy Zivanovic. And he states - and I believe we have to go to the next page in the original - that in the RSK, "nobody can be considered a refugee if they came from Pakrac to Beli Manastir. They should not be treated like that and they should be -- they should not because every citizen who has moved into Baranja has received a house. They have received all the movable and immovable assets of those who had fled to Croatia and they have received land. At the end of the day, they have joined companies and started working or joined our police forces or the military. We think that they can no longer be refugees ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Susa, this is Borislav Zivanovic, the president of the Beli Manastir Executive Council, who is speaking; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it is correct what he says, that Serbs who settled in the SBWS and other parts of the RSK were mobilised into the police and Territorial Defence; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine, I'll repeat my question. It is correct, isn't it, what Mr. Zivanovic says, that Serbs who settled in the SBWS and other parts of the RSK were mobilised into the police and Territorial Defence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I suppose that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And as Mr. Zivanovic points out, Serbs from Western Slavonia were expected to stay in the SBWS; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it was impossible to know yet. Mr. Zivanovic is presenting here some of his personal views, and he says himself that they may be in collision with the law, but these laws could change. Mr. Zivanovic could not maintain that people who had come to the Serbian District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem were permanently residing there. Nobody knew anything about that yet, and I'm sure Mr. Zivanovic didn't either. And ultimately, the people from Western Slavonia themselves were against it. There was nothing controversial about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is another -- well, for the English, it's one page, for the original, two pages, that come from this 20 April session. So I guess it would be another one of these documents we do a .3081 after it. So we would -- we would be tendering into evidence two pages of the B/C/S and one page of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I see, these documents, when was asked from the Prosecution, has the P1597.2. And previous document from the -- from the same minutes was tendered as P3299.301 as far as I recall. And I suggested that all these documents, all the parts of the same documents, be under the same number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There is indeed a possibility of confusion, Mr. Zivanovic, and probably, indeed, the best course of action would be to amalgamate all those different documents into one new documents that we would -- document that we would give just one particular number. Mr. Olmsted, could OTP propose such a new document and confer with the Defence about it, and when you agree, come back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will now admit this -- this one as part of whatever has to be done afterwards for the entirety. So let's give it a new number just as we did the -- did with the previous one with the dot --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: 3081 [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P3306.3081, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, the SBWS and RSK governments never announced a moratorium on the settling of Serbs in the territory under their control, did they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not announce such a moratorium because the Serbs kept coming in ever larger numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, in fact, if we could look at P38 - this is tab 56 - we see the declaration authorising the return of emigrants and displaced persons. We see from this decision, or this declaration, that they kept on inviting Serbs back into the region; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But those were people who had been expelled. This primarily applies to people who had been expelled and had problems with the post-war Communist regime. And for reasons that they deemed unjustified, they had to leave this region, and I believe this is justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 6527. This is tab 152. And these are minutes from the SBWS District Council meeting held on 25 May 1992 in Erdut. And if we could turn to the last page just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us who issued these minutes?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not tell you that because I told you I was no longer a member of this body. In fact, I was never a member of this body. This body was created after the unification into the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and there were people there whom I didn't even know. You see, they are creating new stamps, new letterheads. It's a body that remained there after we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, the English version says that the District Council president was Milan Ilic. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn back to page 1, can you tell us for how long did the central settlement committee operate for? When did it dissolve itself?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably even at this moment it still existed but in a different composition because we had left and some other people came on board after the Republic of Serbian Krajina was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, in fact, the SBWS District Council established a commission to deal with settlement; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was no longer dealing with these affairs at that time. I never read this, so I really can't comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, the effect of moving out -- the moving out of non-Serbs and the moving in of Serbs into the SBWS, was it -- during the 1992 to 1993 period, the SBWS became and remained an ethnic Serb majority territory, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that even before, in the greatest part Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, it had a Serb majority. This did not change significantly the ethnic composition. You're asking me about demographic statistics, and I'm not prepared for that. But I believe that in the largest part of SBWS the Serb population was in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to the conflict in the area that's now known as Western Srem, the Serbs were not a majority, were they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to talk about numbers that I know nothing about. I am not a demographer or a historian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have 65 ter 1098 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now what we have in front of us is a Washington Post article dated 17 May 1992. Now, you have your 2014 statement in front of you, and in paragraph 145 of that statement, you discuss this interview with Blaine Harden from the Washington Post. Do you recall that you discussed that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't see that statement now in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, you have -- your statement is to your left but you don't need to look at it if you recall that you do, in fact, discuss it in your 2014 statement. Now, if we could turn to page 2 of the statement, you were quoted by the journalist as stating: "We have the final say with regard to allowing Croat refugees to come home." That was the official position of the RSK government, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the official position. It was the regulation, and it didn't depend on any conditions being met. By that time, we had already made a decision on the way in which refugees may return.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we turn to page 3 of the -- the document, Mr. Harden writes in this article: "This restoration of the old status quo," and he's referring to the area's pre-war ethnic composition, "is not acceptable to the Serbs, according to Susa, the Serb legal officer here, who said the region should have a Serb majority." That was your position, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see this translation before, and I'm not sure it corresponds to what I really said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let me help you out. In your 2014 statement, in paragraph 145, you say that this statement was taken out of context.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm explaining here exactly why it was taken out of context. If what has been read out to me indeed reads as you say, then it fits into what is written here. I explain why the return of Croat refugees is not possible and what needs to be done before they are able to come back to their homes, and it concerns the project that was covered by UN peacekeeping forces, meaning that the Serbs may also be enabled to go back to their homes. Otherwise, they would have nowhere to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But the bottom line, Mr. Susa, was that the region, in particular, Western Srem, would have to remain an ethnic Serb majority area. And that was your position, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My position was that everyone should return to their homes. If everybody from Western Slavonia had come back to their homes, I don't know what the demographic situation would have been, but it's sure that the Serbs in SBWS would have been that much less numerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at 65 ter 1102. This is tab 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a newspaper article by Ian Traynor dated 18 May 1992. And again we don't have, unfortunately, a Serbian version of this article. But this reporter was in Ilok around the same time as Mr. Harden and reports on an incident in which Kate Horvat came to Ilok -- to the Ilok chateau where your offices were located to inquire about the arrest of her Slovak husband. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that incident. I don't know if she was supposed to ask me for anything concerning this incident, but I know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Further on in the article, he reports that you told about your arrest prior to the conflict, where you suffered injuries to your sinus cavity and received beating while you were being held by members of Croat forces and that you had to leave Vinkovci. Do you recall telling the reporters about that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this at all and I don't remember that detail either. It's correct, but I don't know whether that was the topic of my interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And at the end of the article, Mr. Traynor reports that you declared that the UN should adopt a more realistic view of the objective facts and that among the objective facts, you said that: "Ilok will never again be a town where the Croats and Slovaks outnumber the Serbs." That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that, definitely not. And now, based on this, I now conclude that the gentleman put in the interview whatever he wanted to without my authorisation. As for the Slovaks, that is not realistic because they were a substantial part of the population in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at P28. This is tab 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: These are shorthand notes from the 9 December 1991 meeting of the SFRY Presidency which you attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 65 of the English, page 90 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that you spoke at this meeting, and what we'll need to do is, I think, turn to the next page in the English. As you state at the end of your speech: "The dilemma called Blue Helmets, yes or no, has never existed. We have agreed from the beginning that they should come. The question is where. They have no place there where I heard today that they will arrive. That is the territory under our control. Territory that is our ethnic area." Mr. Susa, that is how you viewed the SBWS, an ethnically Serb area; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody's speaking here only about the SBWS, the discussion here of the entire territory where the Serbs are a majority. This is not only about the SBWS. There was about 100 of us at the meeting, and we were covering the entire territory in Croatia where the Serbs were living as a majority, and the regions were not formed in the same way as they were later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, at this time, the RSK had not been formed. You were a delegate of the SBWS government and that was your perception of the SBWS; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't a government delegate. Everyone from all the Serb regions was invited, so there was discussion as a whole. The plan was not to be applied to us or some parts but to everyone. So what I was talking about applied to the entire area. I don't limit myself anywhere here to the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 1098 and 1102, the two newspaper articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object for 1102 because the witness doesn't know anything about this interview. I think the ... sorry, just to double-check the number. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the second article corroborates the first and it goes to the issue of -- of impeachment and credibility and therefore it should be admitted, with regard to the first one, so that they can be considered together in evaluating this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, but I object. First to paragraph 2. Because as far as I know, the witness was not able to state anything about it also. It is 65 1098.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now I understand that the -- that the Defence is objecting to both newspaper articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, again, Your Honours, it goes to the issue of credibility and they should be admitted at the very least for that purpose. I note that the first article was discussed in this witness's proposed 92 ter statement and he acknowledged that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, I forgot. I had some confusion because this tendering was asked after the documents are already presented. My -- my objection is restricted just to article -- to the 1102, I think, it was, number. On the second article.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, then I go back to my original position that they corroborate each other, they were around the same time as each other, and they relate to the same issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They have nothing to corroborate. The other article is for itself. And Mr. Susa did not respond anything -- said that he doesn't know anything about this interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. Documents are admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1098 will be Exhibit P3307. And 65 ter 1102 will be Exhibit P3308, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be escorted out of court. It's the next break, Mr. Susa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, you took me a little bit by surprise when you asked whether our oral ruling implies that you should pay witnesses yourself for extra proofing days in The Hague. My response would be that you should really know better than to ask the Trial Chamber whether the Defence should pay witnesses. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There is an oral ruling about documents. On the 8th of September, 2014, the Defence filed its third motion to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. The Defence has indicated in the motion that six documents, 1D2595, 1D3642, 1D3644, 1D3645, 1D3646, and 1D3650, are intended for use with DGH-016. The Chamber notes that 1D3646 and 1D3645 were admitted into evidence on 7 and 9 October 2014, respectively. The Prosecution objects to the addition of the remaining documents to the Defence's Rule 65 ter exhibit list on the basis that disclosure was late and it has been deprived of an opportunity to use the documents during Goran Hadzic's testimony. In relation to 1D3642, 1D3644, and 1D3650, the Prosecution additionally objects on the basis that the B/C/S originals of these documents have not been provided. The Defence has replied that the Prosecution has had ample time to digest the documents and the Chamber has allowed amendments to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list even within the Defence was unable to use a document with a prior witness. In relation to 1D3644 and 1D3650, the Defence asserts that the Prosecution disclosed these documents to the Defence without the B/C/S original. After considering the submissions of the parties, the Chamber is satisfied that, taking into account the specific circumstances of this case, good cause has been shown for amending the Defence's exhibit list to include 1D2595, 1D3642, 1D3644, and 1D3650. These documents are relevant and of sufficient importance to justify their addition at this stage of the trial. The Chamber is satisfied that the addition of these documents will not result in undue prejudice to the Prosecution as it has had sufficient time to analyse them before DGH-016's testimony. Further more, additions to a party's Rule 65 ter exhibit list during the course of a case imply that the added documents could not be used during prior testimony. This fact alone cannot justify denying a request to amend a party's Rule 65 ter exhibit list. The Trial Chamber notes, however, that if the circumstances so require, a party can request to recall a witness. With respect to 1D3642, 1D3644, and 1D3650, the Defence shall seek to obtain the B/C/S originals of the documents before tendering them for admission into evidence. The Trial Chamber remains seized of the motion in all other respects. The witness may be brought in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, returning to 1991, the SBWS government held meetings approximately twice a week; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They were held less frequently because there were no conditions. We all travelled from Novi Sad. I think the meetings were not as frequent as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So how frequent do you claim they were?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once every two weeks. Perhaps sometimes it would -- the meetings were more frequent, but, on average, that would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'd like you to take a look at your statement from 1998, which, I numbered the paragraphs for you, and I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 5. And it's probably on the next page because it's about halfway down from the paragraph -- from the beginning of the paragraph. Just turn to ... yeah, flip it over. There you go. The paragraph that's at the top of that page. No. Nope. You had it right before. Yes. Top of that page, yes. Right about there. Yes. It's written: "Since the government was formed at the end of August 1991, these meetings," and you're referring to government meetings, "were held twice a week, which means that we had around 20 meetings by 19 November 1991." Do you see that, Mr. Susa?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Turn to page 3 of the statement. No, I think you're not on page 3. I think you are on page 4. There, now you're on page 3. Now the paragraph that's at the top the page, before paragraph 6, I'm reading from that, and I can't pin-point exactly where in the B/C/S version it's stated, but it is stated --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right, I found it. It's in the middle of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And that's correct, isn't it, that government meetings were held twice a week? And, in fact, the math that you provide is pretty accurate, isn't it, that by the 19th of November, that would mean around 20 meetings.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, it's quite possible. All that was a long time ago. I don't believe we met as often as that. But, all right, I'll allow it. Let's say that we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in your Dokmanovic testimony, you indicated that -- well, before I get there, if we look at this same paragraph, further down, just the next sentence, you said: "Most of these meetings took place in Erdut and occasionally we would go to Baranja." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in your Dokmanovic testimony, you indicated that the SBWS government held a meeting in Ilok on one occasion. Do you recall when that meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember that meeting at all. It's possible that we did have a meeting in Ilok, but I really couldn't tell you when. It had to have been important for some reason for me to be able to remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But as you sit here today, you don't remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. And I understand that a lot of time has passed and that's one of the reasons why I'm referring to your 1998 statement on occasion. Now, the usual number of participants at government meetings was around 25 to 30 people; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, yes. It would be most of the members for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, again, I'm taking this from that same paragraph of your 1998 statement. Now, one of the persons who frequently attended government meetings in his capacity as president of the municipality of Beli Manastir was Borivoje Zivanovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would come to Erdut, but he did not attend the government meetings. When the government session was in Erdut, then he would attend it, in the way that he usually waited in the corridor. All of them did it like that. If I said here that he frequently attended government meetings, evidently this was not formulated properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You didn't correct that in your 2014 statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained in my statement from 2014 how these persons appeared in Erdut and what was their basic objective: To find out information that we would be discussing that day, to take the conclusions with them, and very often to discuss with ministers in the corridors or after the government meetings, to actually do the things that were important for them. This applied to Boro Zivanovic frequently. He didn't have the right to address the sessions or to make any decisions. But even if it did happen that he sat in a seat during one of the sessions, there was nothing for him to do there. He couldn't address the meeting. He couldn't speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's why I'm going back to your statement. Your statement says that he attended, frequently attended, government sessions. And if I understand the last bit of your testimony, you stand by that, that he may have attended but he probably didn't say anything?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He definitely couldn't speak. That was not anybody's right. As for whether he sat there or not, I mean, these meetings were public. There were plenty of seats. They could have sat in. They would not take part in the debate, however, even if they were able to listen to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Local Territorial Defence commanders from different surrounding villages also regularly attended government meetings; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They perhaps attended them in the same way. And not all of them. I think it would be only the people from places where the situation was alarming who would be there. I didn't know them. And it's possible that if the situation was requiring it, things like that would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, in fact, during your Dokmanovic testimony, you testified: "Very frequently, they would sit at the meetings and listen to what was going on. And we wanted to ensure the presence of the public at our meetings because when they would go back to their own villages, they would inform the inhabitants of what we were discussing and what we were preparing to do." You stand by that testimony, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would modify it in this way. There was nothing for them to do at a government meeting. They didn't decide anything or discuss anything. If any of them entered the actual room where the government session was being held, I'm not sure that anybody would throw them out of the room, but their primary goal was to hear the results of decisions that they were interested in. For the most part, they didn't really remain in the room for long, even if they did manage to enter it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In particular, Jovo Rebraca, the Tenja TO commander, Vukasin Egic, the Mirkovci TO commander, and Boro Dobrokez, the Baranja TO commander, would attend almost every government meeting; isn't that correct? And if you want to look at your statement, it's paragraph 6, the next paragraph and it's the end of paragraph 6 and the beginning of paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just reading that. Generally it's correct. But then I would like to touch upon line 2 of the statement because, as I said, the meetings were working meetings, during which many people would come in and many people would go out. Different materials, documents, were being brought in. That's how it looked, more or less. They didn't have their own particular permanent place at these government meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the TO commanders co-operated with the government by informing the government regularly about the situation in their villages; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to give an important correction here. At this stage, they were not commanders of the Territorial Defence. That didn't exist at all. They were just elected by acclamation among their population and they were in charge of making sure that the village guards functioned. It's too early to speak about any form of Territorial Defence. And it's also a major question what a local commander was. These were just local civilians, inhabitants who had taken up weapons in order to defend themselves. They didn't know anything about command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We -- we understand your evidence, Mr. Susa. But, please, focus on my questions and not on, at this stage, correcting your statement. My question to you was simply that local commanders, if you want to call them village guard commanders, that's fine with me at this stage, they co-operated with the government by informing the government regularly about the situation in their villages; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just tell you that the situation was generally very different, and military issues were not discussed, but they were discussed and this was in the context of villages that were under major threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And these local commanders would come to the SBWS government with the problems they were facing in their daily work, such as discipline in their units and food supplies; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did tell us about it. Food supplies and medical, medicine supplies were of primary importance to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And with regard to these problems, they would ask for assistance from the government; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, these local commanders also came to the SBWS government when they experienced manpower shortage and asked you to shift people involved in agricultural or industrial production to perform military functions; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we were the ones who would have been able to help them in that. But if they had engaged people in their area for production and sometimes if we had any influence there, perhaps we did free up some people from production duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, in fact, that what's you say in paragraph 7 of your 1998 statement, that the government relocated people employed in the production sector to the, as you term them, village guards in order to ensure that those villages were adequately defended; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were people that generally belong to those villages, and within that context, this probably did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then at the end of paragraph 7: "At the time, nobody was sent to the JNA anymore. Everyone was staying home and even the ones who were with the JNA came back to defend their homes." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The local commanders had, in fact, two superiors, Mr. Susa: The JNA, who would supply them with food, weapons and wages, on the one hand; and the local civilian authorities on the other hand. And when these local commanders were not able to come to terms with the JNA, they would turn to the SBWS government to complain about their problems; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the local commanders asked the SBWS government to act as arbitrators in the relationship with representatives of the army; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now if we could have P3215 on the screen. This is tab 290. And I think we need to turn to the next page. Yes. And scroll down till -- to the bottom of the original. And I think we need -- we see that it starts on the original on the first page but if we go to the second page --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It was the case that Mr. Hadzic, as the chairman of the Serbian National Council in the SBWS, appointed Ilija Kojic commander of the SBWS TO Staff in July 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I did not have any part in these decisions. I can read them in the same way that you can. This is the Serbian National Council. I don't know anything about its work, and I was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it seems the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that the first page in B/C/S was not seen at the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Susa, but it seems that the interpreters didn't get the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, I was not a member of the Serbian National Council, and it was still a long way before the government was formed. I don't know anything about the work of the council. I can read the decision together with you and comment on it, but I don't think that I could do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware that in August and September of 1991 Ilija Kojic was commander of the SBWS TO?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Kojic was elected as defence minister at the same time that I was elected justice minister. That is what I know. I didn't know what his post was until that time. Nobody ever said anything, in particular, about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware that the SBWS TO Staff had its headquarters at the Borovo Selo primary school?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at 65 ter 1939.24. This is tab 98. And if we can enlarge the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, this is a newspaper publication of an appeal of the defence commander for the Autonomous Region of SBWS and it's dated 22 September 1991, and we can see at the very end of the appeal that it was made by Ilija Kojic as SBWS defence commander.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that at that time that we're discussing now, he was defence minister. As to whether he was a commander at the same time, that is something that I'm not sure about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence commander, I don't know that formulation. I don't know what that could refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could take a look at the sixth paragraph of this document, which is on page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that it states in this announcement that: "The deadline for repatriation is 25 September 1991, after which date we shall apply punitive measures against those that have not responded to our last call to battle." You recall, Mr. Susa, that the SBWS government set that deadline; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I did not get involved in these questions and if you're asking me about things like this, I really couldn't say much about it. But let's say that it is so. I mean, I couldn't tell you anything about this in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's just take a look at one more paragraph in this article. Mr. Kojic, in the next paragraph, appeals to citizens of Serbia to continue recruiting and dispatching volunteers to the territory of the SBWS. Were you aware that that was within the remit of Mr. Kojic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. But the appeal could have been sent by anyone. If he was the one who sent it, I assume that he was authorised to do so. I couldn't really say anything about it now. I don't doubt that he said it, but I am not sure as to what his position was at that time, when he did say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: He further discusses the admittance centre for volunteers in Dalj. And, in fact, there were reception centres for volunteers not only in Dalj but also Sid and Sombor; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. Perhaps it's correct, but I really couldn't say whether it is or isn't. I was not in that area. I did not have information about what you're talking about. I just went to attend the government meetings, and I would return to Belgrade. All of this is something that I don't know anything about. I really couldn't answer with a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's fine, Mr. Susa. We are exploring the basis of your knowledge for your evidence regarding the village guards or the SBWS TO during this September, August period, and it is perfectly acceptable to say: I simply don't know how it was organised or what activities they were engaged in. But you would agree that Mr. Kojic would be in a much better position, as minister of defence, to speak on these issues?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that he would be the one who would need to speak on these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have P22 on the screen. This is tab 12. And I'll draw your attention to the article. I believe it's on the right-hand side of the -- of the original. I think it's the second-to-last column towards the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the article is entitled: "Constitutional law adopted," and it's dated 25 September 1991. And this article reports on the SBWS Grand National Assembly session held on the 25th of September. And that's the session at which Mr. Hadzic, you, and the rest of his ministers were formally appointed to your positions in the government; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 2 on the English, and if you could look at the middle column, I think it's the second full paragraph in the middle column, the article reports that Mr. Hadzic stated in his speech that: "In order for everything to function properly, it was necessary to separate civilian and military affairs. In that respect, the positions of minister of defence and commander of the Territorial Defence are no longer held by one person." Do you recall him making that statement during this assembly session?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember all the things that were discussed. I had a lot of operative things to do at the meeting. I was presenting a lot of laws, so it would be really pretentious of me to tell you that I remember everything that everybody said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, certainly you would recall that pursuant to this decision, Mr. Kojic no longer held the positions of both minister of defence and SBWS TO commander?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know at this assembly he was appointed minister of defence. I said that. What he was before that, I don't know, but I know that after he was only the defence minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And to fill in the position of SBWS TO commander, that position was given to Radovan Stojicic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovan Stojicic, Badza, was the commander of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: He formally assumed that position at this stage, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that was the assembly during which we appointed Radovan Stojicic, Badza, as TO commander. We would need to see that somewhere. I really don't remember much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 6686 on the screen. This is tab 174. And this should not be broadcast to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to confirm that I asked for 65 ter 6686 to be on the screen but not broadcast to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Olmsted, are you telling us that we do the normal thing which is broadcast it to the public but not to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Actually, probably it's better that the public doesn't see it either, so it would just be the parties and Your Honours that can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. And if we could turn to page 8, I'm interested in paragraph 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If it's paragraph 26, I suppose that we should go back one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And then turn to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: There we are. 26. And it's actually at the end of 26. We see -- it just begins there. If we could turn to the next page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Susa, according to this statement, Goran Hadzic nominated Ilija Kojic for the position of minister of defence, a position he held de facto since July 1991, and appointed Badza the SBWS TO commander. That is correct isn't it, Mr. Susa?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That cannot be correct. The ministers were elected in September 1991, not in July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But if you heard what I read, it states that Ilija Kojic was appointed or held the position de facto since July. De facto. Not de jure. De facto, since July 1991. And that Hadzic nominated Kojic for the position of minister of defence subsequently and, hence, on 25 September, he became minister of defence. But what I want to draw your attention to is that, according to this statement, Hadzic appointed Badza, the SBWS TO commander, and that is what I'm putting to you, that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you have such information, but I don't. I never saw that decision or has it ever been published in the Official Gazette that Mr. Stojicic had been appointed to this position. I'd like to see it. And in this specific case, de facto and de jure cannot be different. Because de facto, before September, there was no government whatsoever. These things are obviously very unofficial. If we are talking about anybody's position before September.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 1939.10. This is tab 94. And this can be shown to the witness if ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'll draw your attention to the decision or the document that's label -- numbered 54. And we see that this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn maybe to the second page of the original so we can see who issued it. Of the original -- of the Serbian language one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see this is a demand from Goran Hadzic as -- well, he's the one that issued this decision and it's a demand to the Serbian National Assembly and it's dated 6 July 1991. And one of Mr. Hadzic's demands is that the Srpska Krajina --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I see in the record document 54. But I see -- oh, sorry. That's -- but I see on the screen 55. Of B/C/S. If we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's please return -- I agree. Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. If we could turn back a page, there, to 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that one of Mr. Hadzic's demands is that the Srpska Krajina and the SBWS be annexed to the Republic of Serbia so that Serbia could extend its Territorial Defence to all annexed territories. Mr. Susa, although Serbia did not in 1991 annex the SBWS, it did send its Serbian TO units to the SBWS; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though I told you that I did not participate in any way in the work of the Serbian National Council, you keep showing me decisions of that body, which, as far as I'm concerned, did not have any particular influence except that it created the Grand National Assembly. I don't have any information and I don't want to misinform you. The Serbian National Council, if it had been able to perform the functions of a government, the government would never have been established in the first place. For me, everything begins with my election into that government. That's when I began living in that area. I became familiar with that area then. And you keep talking to me about the Serbian National Council. Of course, I don't mind. You can discuss it with me like with anybody else, but I don't have any particular knowledge about this. And I don't even know if this had any effect to the person to whom it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question to you was: Were you aware that this -- the Republic of Serbia sent Serbian TO units to the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you were also aware that the Republic of Serbia sent Radovan Stojicic to assist the SBWS government in organising its own Territorial Defence; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the SBWS government welcomed the assistance provided by both the Serbian TO units as well as by Badza, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, Goran Hadzic and Arkan had a good relationship in 1991, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you were aware that they very often -- or let me rephrase that. You were aware that very often Arkan would supply security for Mr. Hadzic when Mr. Hadzic would travel through the region where there was potential conflict with enemy forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was in that region, but Arkan definitely did not provide security to Hadzic everywhere where he went. Arkan would travel to Belgrade and Novi Sad where political talks --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Hadzic travelled mainly in the direction of Novi Sad and Belgrade for political negotiations and talks, and Arkan definitely did not accompany him there. Whether he travelled with him somewhere else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to your Dokmanovic testimony. This is 1D2319, page 51 of the e-court pages. You don't have this in front of you, Mr. Susa, so don't bother looking at the document. And unfortunately, we do not have a Serbian version of your transcript, but I'll read it to you. This is on page 51. You were speaking about Arkan and you say: "His relationship with Mr. Hadzic was a good one and very often he would give Mr. Hadzic -- he would supply security for Mr. Hadzic when he would travel through the region where the contact with enemy forces, hostile forces, was a daily occurrence." You stand by that testimony, don't you, Mr. Susa?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it's important how you interpret it. Let it remain the way it is. However, as far as him accompanying Hadzic is concerned, it's not something that I had direct knowledge about. I heard it from other people. But I myself never travelled with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You also knew that Arkan escorted Mr. Hadzic, in particular, when Mr. Hadzic went in the directions of Mirkovci or Tenja; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. But I have no first-hand knowledge of that. I'm again telling you only what I heard from others. I was never with them, either in Mirkovci or in Tenja.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise to the usher, but if we could go back to 65 ter 6686, and, again, this should not be shown to the witness or the public. This time I'm interested in page 5, paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And according to this statement: "Goran Hadzic assigned the Erdut training centre to Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. I do not recall the exact date on which Hadzic made this assignment, but it was before ... 2 October 1991 ... and at the time when Hadzic as SBWS prime minister had the power to take this decision. I believe it was in September 1991." Now, regardless of whether the government approved the decision ultimately, it was Mr. Hadzic who assigned the training centre to Arkan, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he assigned it to him. But you obviously are not aware of what the situation on the ground was like. Nobody should have assigned this training centre to Arkan. Nobody needed to do it. Arkan was sent there, and he was able to take whatever he wanted. It didn't suit me personally that he took it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You allow for the possibility that Mr. Hadzic, in fact, did assign that centre to Arkan; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question arises how he did it. In writing or orally. This decision did not go through the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at P194.140. And this can be shown to the witness and the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what I'm bringing up on the screen, Mr. Susa, is the 21 September 1991 order by Mr. Hadzic appointing Arkan commander of the TO training centre which you looked at during direct examination.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My monitor is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah. And the usher will help you with that. I'm just laying the foundation for you that this is the same order that you saw during direct examination. Now, Mr. Zivanovic drew your attention to the document index number at the top, 1/91, and then he, if you may recall, showed you a 23 August 1991 proclamation of general mobilisation by Mr. Hadzic that had the same index number. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could now turn to P196.140. This is tab 297.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this is a 2nd October 1991 decision by Mr. Hadzic regarding the temporary transfer of assets. This decision, if you look at the upper left-hand corner, contains the same index number, 1/91. So, Mr. Susa, it appears that this same index number was used in August, September, and October 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should be although bodies are very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But all three of these documents were issued by Mr. Hadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we'll let the documents reflect that for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at L57. This is tab 34. And if we could turn to page 12 of the English, page 3 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this is the decision establishing the secretariat of the SBWS government. And if we look under Article 4, we see that within the government secretariat there are three offices, including the office of the prime minister. And if you could take look at Article 7, the head of the office of the prime minister shall manage the work of the office and shall be answerable to the prime minister. Now, who was the head of the office of the prime minister of -- in the secretariat?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was elected sometime in December that year. I see in my mind's eye the picture of that man, but I can't remember the name. It wasn't Jovan Pejakovic, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, this decision was issued fairly early on. It was issued on the 30th of August, 1991. Who performed the role within the secretariat as head of the office of the prime minister until December 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no chef de cabinet until December. Oh, the name is Zrilic. He was the first chef de cabinet and head of protocol. That was in the winter of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And until that happened, Jovan Pejakovic wore several hats, if you will. He was both the secretariat of the government and he assisted Mr. Hadzic with managing the office of the prime minister, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of government did not have any office. Mr. Pejakovic was just the secretary of the government, and even that was too much for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, returning to the SBWS Territorial Defence, or, as you would like to call them, the village guard. You and the other government ministers were aware that members of the Territorial Defence were mistreating non-Serbs in the villages; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those places where there were village guards at the outset, those were mainly majority Serb villages, and they didn't have occasion to stop anyone. They were just defending themselves, and that's the truth about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, if we could have 1D2319 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is again your testimony from Dokmanovic. And I'm interested in page 44. You testified: "Sometimes, unfortunately, that Territorial Defence would mistreat the villagers in the given village -- or given villages." You stand by that testimony, don't you, Mr. Susa?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their villagers. The same villagers who elected them to that position, not Croats. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: They were mistreating the remaining Croats in those villages, weren't they, Mr. Susa?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no specific information about that. It's just an assumption. When such people are concerned, they most often don't discriminate in whom they stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at L1. This is tab 31. And if we could turn to page 62 of the English, page 20 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the decision on the SBWS Territorial Defence joining the SFRY armed forces. This decision, which, I believe, you did look at during direct examination, states that: "The SBWS TO is hereby joining with the SFRY armed forces and becoming part of it." Now, under the SFRY Law on All People's Defence, the term "armed forces" had a particular meaning, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We defined that meaning in such a way as to attach the Territorial Defence to the armed forces, and the Army of the FRY accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, under Article 91 -- and we can call this up if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's L10, tab 2, page 59 of the English, page 16 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Under Article 91, the armed forces comprised of two separate components. You had the JNA, and then as a second component, you had the Territorial Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe that was true of the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the part that was not affected by war. Yes, but the answer is yes, the way it's written in the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And under the law, the JNA and the Territorial Defence had their separate chains of command which reported up to the SFRY Presidency, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: When there are no conditions of a state of war, like here. When imminent threat of war is declared, then the Territorial Defence places itself under the command of the armed forces. In this case, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Susa, that applies if there is an order to resubordinate the Territorial Defence unit to a unit within the JNA, isn't that correct? You needed an order to resubordinate it for the purposes -- for the purposes of combat operations. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did on our part what we were asked to, what we were expected to. I don't know anything about any additional order, if it existed, but this worked. The units were resubordinated to the JNA, and the JNA commanded them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We'll come back to what happened in reality. But I want to focus just on the legal issue here. Now, under the law - and this did not make any difference regardless of what state existed at the time - the republics and the autonomous regions had considerable autonomy over their Territorial Defence as far as managing them, organising them, and supplying them. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are wrong, as far as the state of war and peace is concerned. Or imminent threat of war, which we discussed. If you had given me this law over the weekend, I would have compiled a couple of comments to clarify this. Peacetime and imminent threat of war are divided by a gulf of differences and things work quite differently under these two sets of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Under the law, under the SFRY law that existed at the time, the republics and the autonomous regions had considerable autonomy over the management of their Territorial Defence organisations, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes. In peacetime, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Placing the SBWS TO within the SFRY armed forces would not automatically subordinate them to the JNA but, rather, it would make them equivalent to a republican or autonomous region Territorial Defence; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are giving an interpretation of your own. I don't think it's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, if the intent was to place the SBWS TO under the JNA, the 9 October 1991 decision that we just looked at would have used the term "JNA," but it didn't, did it? It used the term "armed forces."

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was correct. As for this decision taken by the Grand National Assembly, Mr. Koncarevic and a group of his assistants worked together with the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. If they allowed certain flaws in their work, I couldn't change it, and I can't comment on it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be a good time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Susa, it is 2.00. That means the end of the hearing today. We'll expect you to be back tomorrow morning at 9.00, and in the meantime, you remain a witness. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of October, 2014, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.59 p.m.,
